--- title: "Architecture" subtitle: "ESPN cross-league core, the parser layer, and the codegen pipeline" --- `sportsdataverse-py` is built around a small set of reusable cores rather than hundreds of hand-written scrapers. This page summarizes that architecture and the codegen pipeline that drives the production documentation — the part most relevant to a docs-toolchain evaluation. ## ESPN cross-league architecture The cross-league ESPN wrapper surface lives in `sportsdataverse/_common_espn.py`. The pattern is **one core + N thin extensions**: - `_common_espn.py` — ~80 core functions parameterized on `(sport, league)` slugs. Every ESPN URL family is wrapped once (Site v2 / Site v2 alt / Web v3 / Core v2 / Core v3 / CDN). - `_UNIVERSAL_WRAPPERS` / `_NCAA_WRAPPERS` / `_FOOTBALL_WRAPPERS` / `_MLB_WRAPPERS` — tables of `(short_name, core_fn)` tuples mapped onto each league. - `make_league_module(sport, league, prefix, namespace, …)` — iterates the wrapper tables and **registers each one dynamically** in the league module's namespace as `espn_{prefix}_{short}`. Per-league extension modules (`sportsdataverse/{league}/{league}_espn_ext.py`) are four-line files: ```python # sportsdataverse/nba/nba_espn_ext.py __all__ = make_league_module("basketball", "nba", "nba", globals()) # sportsdataverse/cfb/cfb_espn_ext.py — both NCAA + football extras __all__ = make_league_module( "football", "college-football", "cfb", globals(), include_ncaa=True, include_football=True, ) ``` Total cross-league surface: **121 short names** registered across many leagues = **800+ wrappers**. ::: {.callout-important} This dynamic, namespaced generation is exactly what makes auto-introspection documentation tools struggle with this package — there is no static `__all__` of flat names to discover. See the [evaluation write-up](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/sportsdataverse-py/blob/proto/quarto-docs/docs-quarto/README.md) for how that shaped the Great-Docs result. ::: ## The parser layer Every wrapper returns raw `Dict` by default (or, for parser-backed ESPN endpoints, a tidy frame by default). The parser layer turns payloads into tidy polars / pandas DataFrames. There are **six parser modules**, one per data surface: | Module | Surface | |---|---| | `_common_espn_parsers.py` | ESPN cross-league (Site v2 + Core v2 + Web v3) — 30+ dedicated + a 21-section summary dispatcher | | `nhl/nhl_api_web_parsers.py` | `api-web.nhle.com/v1/` modern game-feed | | `nhl/nhl_edge_parsers.py` | `api-web.nhle.com/v1/edge/*` player tracking | | `nhl/nhl_stats_rest_parsers.py` + `nhl_records_parsers.py` | `api.nhle.com/stats/rest` + `records.nhl.com` | | `mlb/mlb_api_parsers.py` | `statsapi.mlb.com` Stats API | | `nfl/nfl_api_parsers.py` | `api.nfl.com` "Shield" data API | **The parser contract is universal across all six modules:** - Return `polars.DataFrame` by default; pandas via `return_as_pandas=True`. - Empty / malformed payloads return a **zero-row frame** instead of raising — so callers can chain without null-checks. - Output columns are snake-cased. ## The codegen pipeline (and what the docs are generated from) Reference docs in the production site are **generated from the same YAML endpoint metadata that drives the wrappers**, via the codegen CLI: ```bash python tools/codegen/generate.py --docs # rewrite the per-league reference subtree python tools/codegen/generate.py --check # CI drift gate: fail on stale generated docs ``` - **Endpoint YAML** lives in `tools/codegen/endpoints/*.yaml` (`espn_site_v2.yaml`, `espn_core_v2.yaml`, `mlb_api.yaml`, …). Each endpoint declares its path, params, `parser:`, and `returns_schema:`. - **`@return` tables** come from `tools/codegen/schemas/*.yaml` (`col_name | type | description`). - **Templates** (`tools/codegen/templates/_reference_block.jinja` + friends) render an 8-section per-function block into markdown for Docusaurus. ::: {#62ef0e36 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

Accurate column lists, but not *actual* `df.head()` output. - **Executable reference** (Quarto here) → the example output a reader sees is the literal frame the code produced at build time. See the hand-written [MLB](reference/mlb.qmd) and [NBA](reference/nba.qmd) reference pages, and the generator-emitted [MLB stubs](reference/generated/index.qmd). ## Ecosystem `sportsdataverse-py` is one package in a multi-language family: - **Python:** `sportsdataverse-py` (this package). - **R sisters:** [`hoopR`](https://hoopR.sportsdataverse.org), [`wehoop`](https://wehoop.sportsdataverse.org), [`cfbfastR`](https://cfbfastR.sportsdataverse.org), [`baseballr`](https://baseballr.sportsdataverse.org), [`fastRhockey`](https://fastRhockey.sportsdataverse.org). - **JS:** `sportsdataverse-js`. Because Quarto is the native literate-docs tool for the R world and also executes Python, a single Quarto toolchain could in principle document the **R and Python** packages with the same run-it-for-real model — a point explored in the [evaluation](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/sportsdataverse-py/blob/proto/quarto-docs/docs-quarto/README.md).
